title: Comprehensive Guide to Measuring and Installing 160mm Threaded Pipes for Farms: From Technical Calculations to Execution
html:
Introduction: The Importance of Precise Pipe Sizing in Farming

In designing drip and tape irrigation systems, one of the most labor-intensive yet critical steps is selecting the appropriate mainline diameter. Plastic pipes with thin walls and threaded connections have become a popular replacement for older metal pipes due to their flexibility and high chemical resistance. The diameter of 160 millimeters is one of the most common sizes for medium to large farms, as it provides a good balance between water flow and fluid velocity, while also appearing logical in terms of installation and maintenance costs.

Many farmers make decisions when purchasing these pipes based purely on guesswork, whereas precise hydraulic calculations are necessary to prevent excessive pressure loss at the end of the line and unaccounted water discharge. This article aims to familiarize you with the logic of selecting 160-pipe sizing by explaining the demand-based sizing process in irrigation.

Technical Principles of Measuring and Calculating the 160 Pipe Diameter

Relationship Between Total Farm Flow Rate and Pipe Diameter

A 160 mm threaded pipe is typically designed to transport flow rates in the range of 60 to 150 liters per minute. If your well or reservoir output flow is below this range, using a 160-pipe may reduce fluid velocity to below the critical limit (approximately 1 meter per second), leading to sludge sedimentation at the bottom of the pipe. Conversely, if the flow rate is significantly higher, fluid velocity increases, and pipe friction causes severe pressure loss.

To calculate, you must first determine the total flow rate required for your drip irrigation network. For example, if your system includes 20 laterals with a flow rate of 5 liters per minute each, the total flow rate is 100 liters per minute. This flow rate makes a 160 mm pipe an ideal option, as it keeps the flow velocity within the safe range (1.5 to 2.5 meters per second). Accurate flow rate calculations sometimes require examining factors such as seeding rate per hectare and plant transpiration intensity to determine the precise water requirement.

friction coefficient and pressure drop along the pipe

PVC and PE pipes have different friction coefficients compared to steel or ductile iron. Technical calculations use the Darcy-Weisbach formula. For a 160 mm pipe, the pressure drop per 100 meters depends directly on the flow rate. For example, at a flow rate of 100 liters per minute, the pressure drop in a 160 mm pipe is approximately 0.5 to 0.8 meters of water column. If your main pipe length exceeds 200 meters, you must perform a precise calculation of cumulative pressure drop to ensure the pressure at the end of the line is sufficient to operate the fittings or drip tapes.

Practical tips for installing and connecting 160 mm threaded pipe

Correct connection techniques (Crimp vs. Threaded)

One of the key advantages of 160 mm pipes for small and medium farms is the availability of threaded connections. However, a critical point is that threads are only applicable to metal-to-plastic joints or screw connections. When joining plastic pipes to each other, always use metal or plastic crimp collars. Overtightening threaded connections on 160 mm pipes causes cracking of the pipe wall due to internal pressure and cold shock. Use Teflon tape or aquarium sealant at the threaded joint to prevent leaks, but never apply mechanical force directly to the pipe body.

Pressure Management on Field Slopes

The biggest enemy of 160 mm pipes is pressure loss caused by steep slopes. If your field is sloped, the 160 mm pipe at the bottom of the field (downhill) faces higher pressure compared to the uphill section. This can cause joint failures or water leaks at downstream points. The solution is to install pressure-reducing valves (PRVs) at the beginning of the main lines. To optimize system performance, it is essential to understand cheap drip irrigation lines and how they operate under variable pressures to prevent water waste in high-pressure zones.

As shown in the table, the 160mm pipe provides the balance point. Choosing a 200mm pipe is more costly and is justified only for farms that require flows above 120 liters per minute without significant pressure drop. However, for most farms in Iran, a 160mm pipe with a standard pumping system is the more economical option.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Is a 160mm threaded pipe resistant to sunlight?

Yes, polyethylene (PE) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes contain UV stabilizers. However, continuous and direct exposure to intense sunlight causes color change and increased brittleness of the pipe wall over the long term. It is best to place the main line in shallow channels or underground, or use protective covers.

What is the allowable working pressure for a 160mm pipe?

The standard working pressure for a 160mm pipe is generally between 5 and 8 bar (depending on wall thickness and manufacturing quality). If your well pressure exceeds 8 bar, you must use a main regulator valve, as pressure above 10 bar can weaken fittings and cause leaks in 160mm pipe connections.

How can I determine if the pipe is correctly adjusted?

After installation, run the system at full flow rate. Use a reliable manometer or pressure gauge to measure the pressure at the beginning of the line and at the end of the line (the last dripper). If the pressure drop exceeds 10 to 15%, you must check whether the pipe diameter is too small or the slope gradient is too steep. Additionally, studying the carrot seed rate per hectare and its irrigation requirements can help you determine a more accurate flow rate for network design.

Summary and Final Recommendations

Using 160 mm threaded pipe is one of the smartest decisions in farm irrigation network design, provided that the measurement and installation process is performed with engineering precision. This size offers high flexibility for farms ranging from 1 to 15 hectares. The key to success is matching the output flow rate of the pump or well with the pipe diameter and accounting for field slopes. By following the principles outlined in this guide and using high-quality fittings, you can prevent unacceptable pressure drops, hidden leaks, and costly repair expenses. Always remember that a good irrigation system is the main foundation for increasing wheat yield per hectare and other crops. With proper water management, you not only reduce costs but also guarantee the quality of your produce.
